newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope to spend few moments at parents' grave.
newsitem.headline: Pope to spend few moments at parents' grave.

text.p: Pope John Paul on Monday leaves behind the ceremony and vast crowds of his Polish pilgrimage to spend a few quiet moments at his parents' grave.

The 77-year-old Pontiff still keenly feels the loss of his mother, father and brother who all died before he was 21. A visit to the grey marble crypt in the southern city of Krakow visibly moved him in 1991.
This occasion is especially poignant as each passing year raises doubts about whether he will ever again return to Krakow, where he spent 20 years as priest, bishop and cardinal.
Chief Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls rejects the idea that the Pope's current 11-day tour in his beloved native land may never be repeated after he leaves for Rome on Tuesday.

"I refuse to accept the notion that this is the Pope's last trip to Poland," Navarro-Valls told a news conference on Sunday, while a Polish bishop noted that several invitations had been made for him to come back next year.
But a future homecoming may take him to other regions than the current route through the west and his beloved southern highlands -- where he was born in Wadowice, near Krakow.

The former Karol Wojtyla's mother Emilia died in 1929 when he was eight. His doctor brother Edmund fell victim to scarlet fever in 1932 and his father Karol died in 1941, two years after Nazi Germans had invaded Poland in World War Two.
After kneeling by the tomb and kissing it in 1991, the Pope said of his father, a retired Polish army officer: "He was both mother and father to me."
Navarro-Valls said about the journey through areas of the Pope's youth: "He is living through a lot of memories."

One that particularly touched John Paul on Sunday was the sudden arrest by Nazi German occupation forces on November 6, 1939, of nearly 150 professors from his Alma Mater who were taken to a concentration camp.

"I was talking to some of them that day...They never went home, they never came back," the Pope said in unprepared remarks at the end of a speech to contemporary professors gathered in the Church of Krakow's Jagiellonian university.
A few minutes later, attending a concert in his honour in the university courtyard, the Pope was seen to touch his eye several times while listening to violin music.
The university, founded in 1364, was shut by the Nazis during World War Two in a drive to destroy Poland's intelligentsia, but students continued to learn underground, including the young Wojtyla.
John Paul's return there crowned a long day starting with a three-hour mass before a crowd police estimated at more than 1.5 million people.
The Pope canonised Queen Jadwiga, who died in 1399 at the age of 25 after helping to spread Christianity to neighbouring countries, particularly Lithuania.

On Monday the Pope was due to celebrate mass in the Cathedral of Krakow's royal castle before visiting his parents' tomb, then tour a heart surgery clinic and bless a church dedicated to St Jadwiga, before spending the night at a remote site in south-east Poland.
